subject: maths
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: The probability scale, outcomes and single-event probability
Combined events: sample spaces, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams
Experimental probability, relative frequency and expected frequency

questions.q: On the probability scale, all probabilities must lie between which two values?
questions.explain: Probabilities range from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), inclusive.

questions.q: What is the probability of an impossible event?
questions.explain: An event that cannot happen has a probability of 0.

questions.q: What is the probability of an event that is certain to happen?
questions.explain: An event that is certain to occur has a probability of 1.

questions.q: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability that it does NOT rain?
questions.explain: The probability of an event not happening is 1 minus the probability it happens, so 1 - 0.3 = 0.7.

questions.q: For an experiment, what is the sum of the probabilities of all possible outcomes?
options: It depends on the number of outcomes
questions.explain: The probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes of an experiment always add up to 1.

questions.q: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4?
questions.explain: The numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6, giving 2 out of 6 outcomes, which simplifies to 1/3.

questions.q: For two mutually exclusive events A and B, how is P(A or B) calculated?
questions.explain: For mutually exclusive events the OR probability is found by adding the individual probabilities.

questions.q: What does it mean for two events to be mutually exclusive?
options: They cannot both happen at the same time
questions.explain: Mutually exclusive events have no outcomes in common, so they cannot occur simultaneously.

questions.q: What does a sample space diagram show?
options: All possible outcomes of an experiment
questions.explain: A sample space diagram systematically lists every possible outcome of a combined experiment.

questions.q: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting two heads?
questions.explain: The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT, so P(two heads) = 1/4.

questions.q: On a probability tree diagram, how do you find the probability of a sequence of events along a set of branches?
options: Multiply the probabilities along the branches
Add the probabilities along the branches
questions.explain: Probabilities are multiplied along the branches of a tree to find the probability of a combined outcome.

questions.q: How is the relative frequency of an outcome calculated?
options: Frequency of the outcome / total number of trials
Total number of trials / frequency of the outcome
Frequency of the outcome x total number of trials
questions.explain: Relative frequency is the number of times an outcome occurs divided by the total number of trials.

questions.q: What generally happens to the relative frequency of an outcome as the number of trials increases?
options: It gets closer to the theoretical probability
It moves further from the theoretical probability
questions.explain: With more trials, experimental relative frequency tends to approach the theoretical probability.

questions.q: A spinner has a probability of 0.2 of landing on red. If it is spun 200 times, what is the expected frequency of red?
questions.explain: Expected frequency = probability x number of trials = 0.2 x 200 = 40.

questions.q: What does it mean for two events to be independent?
options: The outcome of one does not affect the probability of the other
One event always follows the other
questions.explain: For independent events, whether one occurs has no effect on the probability of the other.

questions.q: For two independent events A and B, how is P(A and B) calculated?
questions.explain: For independent events the AND probability is the product of the individual probabilities.

questions.q: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explain: P(both red) = 3/5 x 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10, using the reduced total after the first draw.

questions.q: In a Venn diagram, what does the intersection of sets A and B represent?
options: Outcomes in both A and B
Outcomes in either A or B
Outcomes in neither A nor B
questions.explain: The intersection region contains the outcomes that belong to both A and B.

questions.q: For equally likely outcomes, how is the probability of an event calculated?
options: Number of favourable outcomes / total number of outcomes
Total number of outcomes / number of favourable outcomes
Number of favourable outcomes x total outcomes
questions.explain: With equally likely outcomes, probability is favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled and a fair coin is tossed. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
questions.explain: The die has 6 outcomes and the coin has 2, giving 6 x 2 = 12 combined outcomes.
